message:
SITUATION:
At our basketball academy, after the first 20 free throws of the season we picked the 15 players with the lowest percentages and sent them to a shooting clinic. Over their next 20 attempts, the group's average went from 48% to 61%. The head coach wants to put this in the brochure as proof the clinic works. Our analyst, Ines, suggested, rather hesitantly, that we would expect that group's average to rise on the next 20 attempts even if there had been no clinic at all, because 20 shots is a noisy sample and we chose these players precisely because their numbers were unusually low. The coach thinks that's just an excuse to dismiss good coaching. I think Ines has a point but I don't want to insult the coach. Is she right?

CLAIM:
A group selected for low percentages on a noisy 20-shot sample would be expected to improve on the next 20 shots even without the clinic.

RESPONSE:
**Yes, Ines is right.** What she's describing is **regression to the mean**, and this setup is close to a textbook example of it.

## Why the group would improve anyway

A player's percentage over 20 shots reflects two things: their true shooting ability and luck. With only 20 attempts, luck matters a lot. A true 65% shooter will hit 48% or worse fairly often just by chance (the standard deviation over 20 shots is about ±11 percentage points).

When you pick the 15 lowest scorers, you get two kinds of players:
- Some who really are weaker shooters.
- Some who are decent shooters and had a bad run.

On the next 20 shots, the unlucky ones' luck no longer runs below average, so their numbers drift back up toward their true level. The group average rises even if nothing changed.

**A rough illustration:** suppose the academy average is about 65%. With samples this small, a reasonable guess is that only about half of a player's deviation from the average reflects real skill. A group that shot 48% (17 points below average) would then be expected to shoot around 56–57% next time, without any clinic. That would account for well over half of the 13-point gain. The exact numbers depend on your data, but the direction is not in doubt.

Another factor: early-season shooting often improves for everyone as players get back into rhythm. That would also lift this group without the clinic.

## What this does and doesn't mean

Ines isn't saying the clinic failed. She's saying **this comparison can't tell you whether it worked.** The clinic might be excellent. The 48% → 61% jump just isn't evidence either way, because you'd expect a sizable jump regardless.

## How to find out (and get a claim you can actually use)

1. **Check the other players.** Look at how the rest of the roster changed between their first and second 20 shots. If everyone improved by a similar amount, that suggests rhythm or practice effects rather than the clinic.
2. **Find a comparison group.** If any low scorers didn't attend the clinic (scheduling conflicts, etc.), compare their improvement to the clinic group's.
3. **Use more shots.** Measure on 50–100 attempts before and after. Luck matters much less with larger samples.
4. **Best option next season:** take the low scorers, randomly send half to the clinic, and compare the two halves afterward. Regression to the mean affects both halves equally, so any difference between them is the clinic's real effect.

## Raising it with the coach

You could frame it as protecting the coach's credibility rather than questioning their coaching:

> "Parents and other coaches who know statistics will spot this right away. Picking the lowest scorers and showing they improved is a well-known trap. If we run a proper comparison, we'll get a number nobody can argue with, and if the clinic is as good as we think, it'll show."

This way the coach and Ines are on the same side. Both want a claim that holds up, and a good clinic has nothing to fear from a fair test. A brochure line like "clinic players improved X points more than similar players who didn't attend" is also much more persuasive than the current before-and-after number.
